speeches.speaker: Helen Coonan
speeches.brief: The Trade Practices Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2007 was introduced to amend the Trade Practices Act 1974, creating a second Deputy Chairperson position at the ACCC and amending section 46 on misuse of market power to address leveraging, coordinated market power, and predatory pricing. It also increases the unconscionable conduct price cap from $3 million to $10 million under section 51AC and adds unilateral variation of contracts as a factor for courts to consider.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the government's Trade Practices Amendment Bill was a half-hearted, belated response that failed to adequately strengthen competition law, and announced Labor would move amendments to improve provisions on predatory pricing, recoupment tests, the $3 million threshold for unconscionable conduct, cartel penalties, ACCC powers, and Federal Magistrates Court jurisdiction.

speeches.speaker: Ron Boswell
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Trade Practices Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2007 strengthens section 46 of the Trade Practices Act to address predatory pricing and misuse of market power, following the High Court's Boral decision that made prosecutions difficult. The bill raises the transaction threshold for unconscionable conduct from $3 million to $10 million, creates a small business commissioner on the ACCC, and gains support from groups including NAGA, NFF, COSBOA, and the Fair Trading Coalition.

speeches.speaker: George Brandis
speeches.brief: The speaker moved amendments to the Trade Practices Legislation Amendment Bill, arguing for a code of practice for merit-based appointments to improve integrity, and for new prohibitions on predatory pricing by corporations with substantial market share. The government's amendments targeting below-cost pricing were supported by Labor and the Democrats, while the Democrats' broader amendments on market power and price discrimination were partially supported or rejected.

speeches.speaker: Grant Chapman
speeches.brief: The government opposed all amendments, arguing that its own predatory pricing amendment made Democrat amendment (3) superfluous, that existing case law already covered the "taking advantage" test in amendment (4), and that amendment (5) on price discrimination was unnecessary and could chill competition. It also rejected Family First amendments for introducing "substantial financial power" as a test and an effects test, Labor amendments for rigidifying proof of recoupment and complicating the "taking advantage" test, Democrat amendment (6) on creeping acquisitions as already covered by section 50, and amendments (7)–(9) on unfair contract terms and unconscionable conduct as undermining contractual certainty.

speeches.speaker: George Brandis
speeches.brief: The bill was moved for a third reading, strengthening parts IV and IVA of the Trade Practices Act to restore Australia’s competition laws to world’s best practice after judicial narrowing, with thanks to Senators Murray and Sherry for their contributions.
